utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, good morning everyone in and around the courtroom, this is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today, is Wednesday, the 28th day of May, 2008, good morning to the accused, to the Defence counsel and the Prosecutor and his assistants, to the people helping us out. We have to continue with the cross-examination today. Mr. Prosecutor, you are may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning and good morning Your Honours and to counsel and everyone else in and around the courtroom. Before I continue with the cross-examination, Mr. President, I'd like to bring the Trial Chamber's attention to a filing that was just made this morning and I -- I owe an apology to the Trial Chamber because this was -- it's obviously a very short submission, it relates to the issue of the redirect and it was ready to be filed yesterday, and I simply overlooked it. I forgot to make sure it got filed and so it wasn't filed and so it's now been filed this morning and hard copies have been provided to counsel as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You may proceed. We have received the filing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Cross-examination by Mr. Stringer [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday we were speaking about the citizenship and the constitution and I'd like to shift over a little bit now into a topic that relates more broadly to the issue of Croatia's policy particularly in respect of Bosnia-Herzegovina it's an area obviously that's been a large part of your testimony so far in this case, and I'd like to start at an earlier period, if I may, to ask you a few questions and going back to -- in fact, some writings of President Tudjman from 1981 in a book entitled "Nationalism in contemporary Europe" are you familiar and I can direct to you an exhibit 1D 00401 which has a part of that book that I'd like to ask you about, 00401, 1D. I think the usher is going to be -- if I could ask the usher to assist the witness with Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, I believe it would be very useful if you do so actual the counsel would always indicate in which binder the document is to be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will do my best. I'm not sure exactly which binders necessarily the Defence Exhibits are in but we'll do our best.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Binder 1. It's in binder 1 for the Defence but I think -- I believe there should be blue binders. We tried to make it easy for everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: For what it's worth I'm being told that the Defence Exhibits that are in the black binders have been rearranged so that they are in strictly numerical order and so which ever works easiest for the usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, then, do you have Exhibit 1D 00401 in front of you there? It's a reference to Dr. Tudjman's book.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I haven't completed my answer yesterday to Their Honours question in relation to the earlier document that was shown here, I'd like to complete that, please. His Honour Judge Prandler --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could just interject and I do so -- I don't mean to be rude. It's in fact my intention to bring you back to the transcript that Judge Prandler was asking about yesterday. Judge Prandler, as he often does, anticipated what I was going to do before I did it, and so if it's acceptable to you, my preference would be to work through two other documents and then we will come back to that same transcript which was the transcript from December of 1991. Would that be acceptable?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite all right, but I should like to finish the answer I started giving yesterday and I believe that was quite an important topic. This can take place whenever, now or when you go back to that issue again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's save that for later then, when we reach that part of the examination. So now if you could take the excerpt of Dr. Tudjman's book and I can read just a few short passages that I'd like to ask you to comment on. Are you familiar with this book by Dr. Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm looking at a passage that's found on page 113, this is the English version, in which Dr. Tudjman writes -- he's writing about how the Vojvodina having become a part of Serbia perhaps could be a model or should have been a model for Bosnia-Herzegovina or parts of it becoming a part of Croatia back in previous times. He writes, "Furthermore, Bosnia and Herzegovina were historically linked with Croatia and they together comprise an indivisible geographic and economic entity. Bosnia and Herzegovina occupied the central part of this whole separating southern Dalmatian from northern Pannonian Croatia. The creation of a separate Bosnia and Herzegovina makes the territorial and geographic position of Croatia extremely unnatural in an economic sense and therefore in the broadest national-political sense, very unfavourable for life and development and in the narrower administrative sense unsuitable and disadvantageous." Would you agree with me, sir, that even going back to 1981 some 10 or 12 years before this conflict, Dr. Tudjman's views were that Bosnia and Croatia as a state entity was not suitable or was unnatural in respect of the -- its position with Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not what Dr. Tudjman wanted to communicate here. He emphasised the territories of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the one hand, and Croatia on the other in terms of territory and you can see easily on the map, he's not talking about any sort of unification in terms of a state or divisions, for that matter. He's indicating certain truths here and he's talking about the fact that one part of Bosnia-Herzegovina was, yes -- yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The truth was that his view was that based on its historical and other links, that this separateness was unnatural and it was not advantageous for Croatia, would you agree with me on that? Setting aside whether he had any intentions or views about changing borders, would you agree with me that his view was that this separateness was unnatural based upon the historical and geographical links between the two countries?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, until the European Union came into play or emerged. Many of the problems mentioned by Dr. Tudjman had been solved or will be solved through the European Union. Borders are no longer a problem or the problem of Bosnia being in the midst of Croatia. This is all resolved through the European Union. I believe that one needs to make a distinction between the views held by Dr. Tudjman before the European Union became a reality, so to speak, because the European Union would resolve all these.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. All right. So at least as of this time into 1981 and up until the time of the European Union, you agree with me, then, that Dr. Tudjman considered the separateness of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia to be unnatural and not in the best interests of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would use the term "ties" rather than separateness because the countries are in a way connected and drawn one toward the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he said, "... an individual geographic and economic entity ..." do you share that view in terms of "Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia as historically linked comprising an individual geographic and economic entity"? Do you share that view?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just casting a glance at the map will show that this is self-evident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to take you to another exhibit and again I'm going to ask you, this is a little bit more in terms of background before we get into more specific details on the policy, and the next exhibit is marked P10402, that's a Prosecution Exhibit, 10402. While that's being located, Mr. Ambassador, I'll tell you what it's about and it might make your -- just to keep us moving. We're looking at a lot of books in this -- in the various examinations. Are you familiar with the book that was written after the conflict by your former boss, the former minister for foreign affairs, Mate Granic? Are you familiar with the book that he wrote?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there are some things that he's written in his book that I wanted to direct your attention to and ask you to comment on as well. And the first of those, we have an English excerpt of the book which is limiting what I'm going to be talking about here. There is a section of his book which you should have in front of you in the original language under the heading "Gojko Susak" do you see that? You have that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as you indicated yesterday, Mr. Susak, like yourself, was an emigre, that is, he is someone who had been living outside of Croatia and who returned to Croatia during the years of the war.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The point that needs to be made is that I didn't know of Mr. Susak while he was abroad. We met for the first time during his visit to Venezuela in 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And I'm not suggesting otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, could you tell us when this book was published? I fail to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to have to try to get that answer for you because I don't have it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: We'll do this later too?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I can be of assistance. I believe it was around 2006 keeping in mind that Dr. Granic is heavily involved in Croatian politics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. But I expect Mr. Stringer to give us a precise answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, I will, Your Honour. We'll provide the actual cover page as part of the exhibit, and I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's a reference here actually to the time when Mr. Susak held the position that you took over from him which was the position of Minister For Emigration or minister for the diaspora and here in this first paragraph regarding Susak, he writes, "Mr. Susak was formerly the Minister for Emigration but in reality, his main task was to collect money for defence and facilitate the return for emigrants especially former political emigrants." Do you see that passage?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now you just indicated that you met Mr. Granic, I believe, for the first time when he came to Venezuela in 1990.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I said that about Mr. Susak, not about Mr. Granic. I came into contact with Mr. Susak for the first time when he came do Venezuela in 1990 as the Minister For Emigration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That was my mistake. When he came to Venezuela, was one of the objectives to meet with you and try to encourage yourself to return to Croatia to contribute to its defence?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely not. At the time, I had no intention of going back to Croatia. I decided to go back to Croatia when I saw that it had been attacked, that aggression had been committed on Croatia. It had nothing to do with Mr. Susak's visit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'm going to skip ahead a little bit to page 4 of the English excerpt and direct you to a passage that relates to the time when the Greguric government was dissolved. I don't know if you can find that in the original language version there. And Granic writes "That the Minister of Defence," who at this time was Susak: "The minister of Defence became Tudjman's right-hand man in all operations in Bosnia-Herzegovina and he probably did not like the idea of having to explain his moves to the ministers some of whom like Budisa and Tomac were members of the opposition. His opposition to the Croatian policies in Bosnia and Herzegovina cost Tomac the post of ambassador in Slovenia which he had been promised." Now, my question here Mr. Ambassador, is that then after Susak became Minister of Defence and after the Greguric government was dissolved, do you share the view, is it true that in fact Susak remained Tudjman's right-hand man as Minister of Defence in respect of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I have to make a correction. The government of Mr. Greguric was not dissolved, it was the democratic unity coalition government which existed until the month of August, and I was a member of that government. It was not dissolved, it was replaced by a new government. The role that it had was that all the parties participating in that government should stick together as long as the war lasted. When the war ended and UNPROFOR forces arrived in Croatia, Dr. Tudjman decided, as the president of the republic, and Mr. Greguric as the prime minister that the government can be as such, as a coalition government changed and it was not dissolution, not the term that you used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In any event, then, when Mr. Susak was Minister of Defence at this time, do you agree with Mr. Granic here when he indicates that it was Susak as Minister of Defence who was Tudjman's right-hand man in all operations in Bosnia-Herzegovina? I'm just asking whether you agree with that or not?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not agree with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And if you were in a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one follow-up question, if you don't mind. Mr. Ambassador, the Prosecutor asked several questions regarding the government, the Ministry for Emigration of which you were responsible. I have a very and purely technical question. You were a minister for a while before you became the ambassador of Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina. When you were a minister, would President Tudjman gather his ministers in official meetings with an agenda each time and with every minister speaking? Was there a transcript or minutes of the ministerial meeting? Is that the way it would work or did it work differently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is how it worked. There were three types of meetings: Government meetings, which included government members only and was chaired by Prime Minister Greguric. Next, there were government meetings chaired by Mr. Greguric and involving only some of the major ministries, I wouldn't be able to tell you which those were at the time. I attended government meetings when all of the government ministers were there. Finally, there was the third type of meeting which was chaired by the president of the republic himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In government meetings chaired by the prime minister, by Greguric, was there an agenda and were there minutes of the government meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I personally didn't see there were any minutes. I came to that conclusion due to the fact that when Mr. Greguric published a book about his activities during his term of office while he was the prime minister of the government of democratic unity in which all parties participated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question. During these government meetings, was the defence minister present, and if he attended these meetings, were military matters addressed at a governmental level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The government meetings were not attended on many occasions by Mr. Susak because there were lots of things going on relating to the defence of Croatia so instead of attending the meetings personally, he would delegate his deputy, but I cannot tell you exactly who stood in for Mr. Gojko Susak in these meetings. He did attend, however, on a couple of occasions. It is well-known that Mr. Gojko Susak is not a man of many words and he didn't take much part in these exchanges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about the prime minister, did he not address military issues or did he consider that this was within the remit of Mr. Susak, the defence minister together with President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look, Mr. Greguric was the war-time prime minister of democratic unity and Mr. Susak was within his jurisdiction. Normally, in government meetings, he would tackle defence issues in Croatia. For example, once Dr. Greguric said that we, the ministers, should go outside Zagreb into the field and see what was happening there in order to get the better feeling of what this war was about. What I mean to say is that Mr. Susak was subordinated to Mr. Greguric just like me to President Tudjman because under this constitutional system, both the President of the republic and the prime minister had a lot to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There's a correction that needs to be made that Greguric is subordinate to -- Susak was subordinate to Greguric and Tudjman - that's what I'm told - that the gentleman indicated, perhaps we can clarify that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, could you please clarify that point, Witness. We have a sentence that's not very clear. Can you please clarify again what happened in terms of subordination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under the constitution, the president of the republic had certain functions. The same applies to the prime minister. And we, who were ministers in the government of democratic union in which all parties participated equally were subordinated first of all to the prime minister and then president of the republic was above the prime minister. Therefore, to the president of the republic as well. For example, if he -- if Mr. Greguric could convene a government meeting, we would attend. He was our subordinate. However, when we were invited by President Tudjman he himself had certain duties, and he was in charge of certain things related to the government.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: "He was our superior."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At one point, you said that it was a semi presidential regime. This can be a source of confusion. Should we understand that the government enjoyed a certain degree of autonomy with respect to the president or was it the case that the government had no autonomy whatsoever because the regime was of a presidential nature and because the president was the one who told the prime minister and the ministers what they had to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. At the beginning, I said that it was a coalition government in which all political parties participated. Therefore, the role of the prime minister should have been that of a -- should have been coordinated with all Croatian parties because that was the time when all the Croatian parties pulled together in order to defend Croatia from the Greater Serbian aggression. I don't know if this is clear enough. My immediate boss was Dr. Greguric but according to the constitution, Mr. Tudjman also had a say in these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So you are telling us that this was a coalition government, that several political parties were represented within the government, and this coalition government was working under the authority of President Tudjman in full agreement. Is that what you're trying to tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not what I said. I said that my immediate boss, superior, was Dr. Greguric, the prime minister and since all the political parties participated in this Croatian government except for those who did not reach the threshold because these were minor parties that did not have representatives in the parliament, all the other parties took part in this democratic unity government, wartime democratic unity government of Dr. Greguric and the participation of Dr. Tudjman was partial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a point of clarification. If we listen closely to the Croatian, he's saying the president of the government which is being translated as prime minister so as long as we understand that prime minister is president of the government but that's what the gentleman is indicating the correct terminology which is president of the government as opposed to president of the state, but I think we're using prime minister, but to me it doesn't make a difference just as long as everybody understands.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I mean if this is a translation issue or an interpretation issue, we'd like to hear it from the interpreters because it's clearly an important issue and I appreciate counsel's clarification but I just want to make sure that it's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ambassador, according to you, was Mr. Greguric the prime minister or the president of the government? In your own language, how would you express that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] President of the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So we have the following situation: Mr. Tudjman is the president of the republic and Mr. Greguric is the president of the government. In other words, he has the position of prime minister, he fulfills the duty of a prime minister or am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We do not have the term "prime minister" in Croatian, the term we use is the president of the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One final question before I give back the floor to Mr. Stringer, but you understand that my questions deal with very significant issues, that's why I keep asking question after question. In your political system, are policies defined by the government and by its president or are the policies of the country defined and determined by the president of the republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It depends on the type of the government, whether it was a single-party government, that is to say, the most powerful party such as the HDZ, or if it was a coalition government such as the one I was part in. In a coalition government, Dr. Greguric had to put together all the aspects and inputs of the participating parties in the government, major parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, if I understand you correctly, that we have to make a distinction between the case where you have a government made up of representatives of a single party and the case where you have a coalition government. If I understand you correctly when there is a single party in the government, the president comes from the same party and they follow the same policies but when you have a coalition government, this government defines the policies of the country and the president of the republic has to follow this course. Is that what you're explaining to us? Because you see so far, we've not dealt with these issues but since you're here and you were part of the government, you may help clarify this for us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I try to be very clear because I participated in a coalition government made up of all the parties during the war and that is how I became a member of the government. At the time, I wasn't a significant political figure. The point was to rally together all the important personalities in order to make Croatia capable of defending herself from the aggression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are not answering my question fully. When the coalition government would meet --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat my question. I wanted to know the following: What about if the coalition government defined or decided on a policies -- if I understand, President Tudjman could not go against that policy because the coalition government decided on the policies. That's what I wanted to know. When you had this coalition government with Mr. Greguric as a president, and when you decided something, did Mr. Tudjman have to accept your decisions or was Mr. Tudjman in a position to say, "Okay, that's your opinion but I have a different view of the situation and I'm going to make the decision"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me be specific in answering your question. During the term of office of the coalition government, in most cases or almost in all cases, Mr. Greguric was the one to make decision based on the consensus among the parties. I hope I was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you were very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to ask maybe the same question in a different way. Can you give us an example or more than one example where Mr. Tudjman had an intention, a political intention which then the government refused to follow so that in the end, the will of the president was not realised in Croatian politics.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can say that there were such differences. You want me to give you specific examples. I would need some time to think about the instances where there was no full consensus or full understanding of the president of the government or the president of the republics but I know that there were differences. Now, how these differences were eventually resolved and ironed out, I cannot give you any details in that respect because I was a member of the government and Greguric was the main man in my view, and I never by passed him in order to talk to Tudjman. The normal procedure was ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That goes beyond what -- Mr. Stringer, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to follow up on a few questions, can you tell us, Mr. Ambassador, what was the term, period of time in which the Greguric government of democratic unity was in existence?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war, during the attack which means since August 1991 until August 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in August of 1992 or approximately during that time, did the elections take place that you referred to a few minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall mentioning elections. I didn't say anything about elections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I had used the word the Greguric government was dissolved and you, I thought, indicated that it wasn't dissolved and that -- but that it changed as a result of elections.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mention the word "election" but a new government came and for the most part, it was made up of people from the HDZ and that was the result of the elections because the HDZ was the most powerful political party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So beginning in August of 1992, the structure was one that was less of a coalition and more of a single-party government?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but as far as I can remember, there were always a few ministers who were not members of the party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Like any system in which the government is largely a single-party government of which the president is a member, the president of the republic would have had enhanced powers, increased powers after the election, after the change of government in August of 1992. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with that but I would just like to add that the government's policy was never solely Mr. Tudjman's policy, it was under various influences especially with regards to the international community and so on. In other words, the state policy was created -- we keep talking about Tudjman. Tudjman was not a God. Tudjman was what he was according to the constitution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now -- and I think the point about influence and who was influencing the president is an important one and I'd like to ask you more about that. Moving down a little further in this passage from Mr. Granic's book, Mr. Granic makes reference to a conversation that he had with President Tudjman at the time that Tudjman offered him the post of foreign minister. And Granic says, "You will have complete freedom to choose your assistants but we will have to talk about ambassadors. Do not forget that according to the constitution, I am the only boss and that you have to come to me for a problem because foreign affairs are not a matter for government," he told me firmly. Then he continues, he says, "He told me that we would especially be discussing Bosnia and Herzegovina and then added, and this is a quote attributed to President Tudjman, 'Mate, only Gojko Susak is in charge of the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina.'" So then on this question of influence, isn't it true, Mr. Ambassador, that it was Gojko Susak that was in the strongest position to exert influence on President Tudjman in respect of his policy on Bosnia-Herzegovina particularly the Croats there?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm doing my best to give you an answer but if I am not accurate enough, I would kindly ask you to repeat certain portions of your question. Gojko Susak was the minister of defence over the years. Why was he the defence minister. Probably because either he was doing his job properly or not, but let us not forget that Mr. Mate Granic was also in a certain way the boss to him. So what Mr. Mate Granic is saying here ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry for cutting you off and we do want your full answer but I'm hoping that we can be a little more succinct. As defence minister, wasn't Gojko Susak the person influencing and impacting most President Tudjman's policies in respect of Bosnia-Herzegovina Croats and I say that because we all know and accept that the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina was one that impacted the defence interests of Croatia. So I'm not making any negative inferences, I'm just asking you: Wasn't it Gojko Susak as Minister of Defence who have been the position most influential in terms of Dr. Tudjman in respect of Bosnia-Herzegovina policy?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me be specific. There were some of us who had certain influence on Dr. Tudjman apart from Mr. Susak. I, as a minister and not only as a minister, but also as an ambassador later and a "dolje" of the diplomatic corps in Bosnia-Herzegovina had to say certain things. It was not just Mr. Susak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm not suggesting that. But I am suggesting that it was Susak who had the greatest influence. That seems to be what Mr. Granic is saying here. Maybe you don't know. If you don't know the extent of Mr. Susak's influence, you can say that.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm going to say this: In the context and the scenarios of the events, it may have been the case that at certain points, someone had a stronger inference or a weaker or lesser inference but there was no exclusive inference coming from any quarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about exclusive influence, I'm asking simply whether you agree with the proposition here that it was Susak excerpted the most influence or who appeared to have the greatest responsibility in terms of the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Wasn't he the most influential among a number of people?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, the witness has answered it. He said that over time, the person who has influence may change. It has been already answered, in my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, on several occasions, not just once, the witness stated that influence is a very subjective thing and the witness stated that according to him, several people were in a position to have an influence on Mr. Tudjman and that Mr. Susak was not the only one in that position. That's what I thought I understood listening to the witness. We may ask him to clarify that for us. Witness, we do not want to be wasting any more time. Can you please tell us the following: In your view, did Mr. Susak have some influence on President Tudjman or did other people have an influence on him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] President Tudjman would listen to many people in various meetings which can be seen from the transcripts. Therefore, there were us who tried and participated in creating the Croatian state policy towards Bosnia and Herzegovina. Have I been clear in this that this involved a number of people?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ambassador, I think you always navigate around the question the Prosecutor asks you and that is: Here, Mr. Granic says Susak had the main, not the only, the main, the strongest influence. And the question is: Yes or no, do you agree? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me put it this way. In various different periods of time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This is not very polite but it's the style of the Tribunal and in cross-examination, the counsel may ask a question to which there is one or two or three or four questions as Mr. Karnavas has many, many times recalled, yes, no, I don't know, I don't remember. Could you please answer with one of these words?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, just one intervention. With regard to many questions, we have tried to suggest to the person putting questions to specify the time that the question refers to. What I think the witness is saying is that at different times, various people had different level of influence and if you want to be more specific, and if you want to insist on Susak's influence on Tudjman, could you please be more precise and specify the time period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, you should get an answer to your question. It may relevant to explain when this happened, the question of time because it could be "yes" for one period and "no" for another. Could you specify your question based on the year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm speaking about the period after the -- beginning of August 1992 in which the primarily HDZ government took -- HDZ party took the government and continuing through 1993. So approximately a year and a half period, August of 1992 to -- through all of 1993. Isn't it true that Susak was Mr. President Tudjman's right-hand man if I can put it that way in terms of Bosnia-Herzegovina policy particularly Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would -- I have to say yes or no. Well, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't agree with the suggestion here by Mr. Granic that Susak was the right-hand man or that he -- that he had the greatest influence on Tudjman? Let me ask you why -- because you're an ambassador toward the latter part of 1992 and then you went down to Bosnia-Herzegovina. It just seems to me that Mr. Granic was in a greater position to know what were the relative roles of the members of the cabinet, Mr. Susak, Mr. Granic, himself, and the others. That's why I say this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, that is the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true that Mr. Granic is in a better position to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. I would like to put forth an observation. In order for the witness to be able to answer the question, he would have to be familiar with the relationship between Granic and Susak. In the HDZ government, they were the two people who were working at cross-purposes and who confronted. I just wanted to propose this comment by way of helping further clarify the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I got an answer from the witness, he denied my -- he did not agree with my assertion. I think I'll just take that and move on to the next point. With your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move on, yes. Mr. Praljak, you're on your feet, why are you on your feet? The Prosecutor is moving on to another subject. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I simply fail to grasp the meaning of the word "influence." I don't understand the term influence. Can somebody help me and clarify the meaning of the term influence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, it is a word that was used by the Prosecutor. When you call your own witnesses, you can clarify the concept of influence. Well, your intervention is recorded in the transcript, but it does not call for further comment. Please proceed, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, there's a following section that falls under the heading "government of democratic union and BH," and I just want to take you to one passage there in which Mr. Granic mentions Mr. Mate Boban. I take it you know who Mate Boban is. I'm not sure if we've talked about him yet?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He says, "Boban was a very narrow-minded man full of hatred for the Bosniaks. He supported Bosnian Serbs believing that he could enter into an agreement with them regardless of the criminal policies of Karadzic, Mladic and their assistants. It was clear to me that he was the biggest obstacle to peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina. At meetings, he never spoke about the Bosniaks or Muslims, but only used words like Turks or 'balija' for Bosniaks." These are very strong words, in my view, Mr. Ambassador and I'd like to ask you to comment on that. First of all, as a preliminary question, tell us how frequently or how regularly did you have dealings yourself with Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you in a position to --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I be allowed to explain, please? I already said that I worked at the level of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was the -- in charge of the Croatian policy vis-a-vis Bosnia and Herzegovina. Mate Boban and the issue surrounding him is the internal matter of Bosnia and Herzegovina and obviously I did not come into contact with Mr. Boban; but I did see him at some meetings and on one occasion, I explicitly at President Tudjman's request, I went to see him and I can tell you when that happened and why.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why don't you tell us that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Stringer. I have full respect for you but I must tell you this. I, myself, asked a question of the witness. I asked him how many times he had met with Mr. Boban and he answered. He said once. You are asking the question again. So, that's one of two things. Either he told me when he answered my question and then you have evidence that he lied then or you sort of follow up on my sentence saying by saying -- you said to the Presiding Judge that you met him once, could you specify the circumstances. Because if you keep repeating the same questions, asking the same questions, it's a waste of time. It's useless. It's pointless.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President. I had -- I forgot apparently now two things from yesterday, one was the filing and the other was the question that you'd already asked of the witness. So with your permission, if we could just recall that testimony that there was one meeting, I think it does impact then on whatever opinions he might have or comments he might have on the remarks of Mr. Granic here and with your leave, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador if I could just ask you to tell us what you can about the meeting you had with Mr. Boban, where was it and when was it. Tell us your impressions of him whether you agree with the characterisation given by Mr. Granic.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Please allow me to read what Mr. Granic said about him. Can you please refer me to the page where I can find it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can -- it is under the heading, there's a heading called "Government of democratic union and BH"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It says that it's page 70 in the translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have that? Page 70. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the translation? I don't have the translation before me. I have it only in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, well --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there is a translation as well. What page again, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I thought -- you wanted to look at the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: In the Croatian, it is the last sentence on page 70. The last sentence of the Croatian version is, "Izmedzu nas nikada nije ..."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It begins with the words, "We were never close ..." I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then it begins, "Boban was a very narrow-minded man."

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I answer, please? With regard to the first part of this statement of what Mr. Granic wrote that they were never close and they advocated completely opposed positions, this is completely correct and I witnessed that myself. However, when Mr. Granic portrays Boban in the way he does, listen, I really never gave it much thought. I did not have anything to do with defence. Granic was my boss and I listened to him and I reported to him. I'm aware that there were conflicts between Dr. Mate Granic and Mr. Susak. I'm aware of that. I wouldn't be able to give you any details thereof.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a clarification here. I think you just indicated that there were conflicts between Dr. Granic and Mr. Susak and I was asking you about Mr. Granic and Mr. Boban. I wasn't sure if you intended to address that or ...

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Granic and Boban? I don't know how much contact they had at all because Granic worked through me. Granic was the Minister of Foreign Affairs and I was his extended hand in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the state level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Then is it fair to say that in general terms during the period during which you were at the ambassador to Bosnia-Herzegovina, you did not concern yourself very much with Mr. Boban or with the leadership of the HDZ party in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that this is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicated yesterday, I believe, that you had some informal discussions with Dr. Prlic about economics but the impression that you did not have a lot of substantive dealings as well with Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I object to word substantive, economics is a substantive matter in the middle of the war when Dr. Prlic was involved in setting up the economic infrastructure for the region, so I wouldn't put it that it wasn't substantive.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I just had the impression that -- and he can clarify that the ambassador said that he had had some informal discussions with Dr. Prlic about economics because it was an interesting issue but these were not formal discussions. That's -- that was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look, it depended on Dr. Prlic's function. At one point, he had been elected as the prime minister of Bosnia and Herzegovina. When he was elected prime minister, then I could and did have official contacts especially after the Washington Accords when Dr. Prlic became the vice-president of the government and the Minister of Defence of both the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Federation. At such moments, I had official relations with Dr. Prlic and I had discussions with him when I deemed that those were necessary and I usually contacted him on economic matters because he was the person in charge of all the economic matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, allow me to intervene because there's a problem of semantics. You said that Mr. Prlic was the prime minister, so let's be specific here too. Was he prime minister or was he president of the government, in your view? What was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are two periods in question here. The first one when he participated in the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina for a very short period of time. That was after the Medjurgorje Accords on the 18th of -- I believe it was in August or thereabouts during the peace mission undertaken by Dr. Tudjman that was a very short period of time when he became the vice-president to be very specific of -- the I apologise. I can't remember what his title was. He was either president or vice-president of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and later on I remember this very well after the Washington Accords for a long period of time, he was the vice-president of the government and the Minister of Defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. At that time, I could deal with him officially and talk to him officially because I was the ambassador of Croatia before the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave one additional matter. At page 26, my learned friend asked the witness to describe his meeting with Mr. Boban. He wasn't actually given the opportunity to answer that question. I just raise it because it was asked and it wasn't answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it escapes me, but yes, I'm sure Mr. Khan is right. The question was not answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. I had actually intended to bring the witness back to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I do, just while we're talking about titles, is it true or do you know if Dr. Prlic was the president of the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council during 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know, I know this exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, on the last answer, Witness, when you said that Dr. Prlic was vice-president, I think, Minister of the Defence in the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, could you tell us what period of time you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the Washington Accords, immediately after the Washington Accords. At that time, I participated in the implementation of the Washington Accords in Sarajevo. I had a very big role in that. The first meeting with Prlic was regarding his ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. You've answered my question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Boban was the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna during 1993 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Boban was also the leader of the HDZ party in Bosnia-Herzegovina as well, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was the leader of the HDZ party in Bosnia because Dr. Tudjman, as the leader of the party, had approved his taking that position. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to object -- I object to that. There's no foundational question as to that. Is this -- is he putting this to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true that Mr. Boban was president of the HDZ party in Bosnia-Herzegovina because he was approved for that position by President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Tudjman was the president of the HDZ in Croatia. The HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina had a different structure and a different trajectory. Mr. Tudjman was in a position to possibly suggest things to them but he could not order them anything because they were a democratic institution in which people in Bosnia and Herzegovina could elect people, leaders, presidents. Several of them preceded Boban, several of them followed Boban.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next exhibit is the one that Judge Prandler showed you yesterday. It's one of the presidential transcripts P0089. If the usher could assist with that one, I would be grateful. Now, while that document's being located for you Mr. Ambassador, just to recall, this is a transcript of a meeting that occurred in Zagreb on the 27th of December, 1991. And as you indicated yesterday and we know, you were not present at the meeting. I believe, however, that in December 1991, you had just become the minister for the diaspora. Am I correct on that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now I just want to follow up with a couple more questions on the passages that are in this transcript recognising that you weren't present. 0089. And I'm going to direct you -- well let me just -- to inform you while it's being located, this is a meeting in which President Tudjman has accepted guests who are the -- from the HDZ party delegation from Bosnia and Herzegovina and that's who is present at this meeting and there was a reference yesterday as you might recall to Mr. Ignac Kostroman who was present. As well, there were other members of the leadership of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina who were also present there, Mr. Boban --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Incidentally while we're looking for these documents, if he's going to be asked an opinion opine on something where he wasn't attending, I do so based on and I ground my objection on the basis that on a very similar situation where I had Dr. Zuzul here and I was asking the question, Judge Trechsel, you objected on the grounds that I was asking him to be an expert. Frankly, I took exception to your observation but nonetheless, I think that it fits here as well so I don't wish to debate the issue I think I respect you highly, I think we can agree to disagree at some times, however, I think that is the same situation we are faced here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Good point, Mr. Karnavas, I fully take that but we have not heard the question yet so why don't we wait for the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may add something that is very relevant with regard to Mr. Karnavas's objection and your decision with this regard. If my learned friend from the Prosecution is allowed to embark on the line of questioning that they wish to put to the witness, then I would kindly ask to lay some foundation for the questions in order to see whether the witness is in a position to answer the questions. We'd like to hear some basic elements as to what was happening in Croatia in December 1991 and what was happening in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the same time because if we do not understand the context, if we don't know what in real life was happening at the time, we cannot be objective and we cannot provide an objective interpretation of any conversations including this one. This conversation cannot be understood without the context and the position that these people were in, their motives, why they arrived in Croatia, what the international positions and interventions were taking place at the time. I believe it is absolutely pointless to embark on a discussion especially in view of the fact the witness wasn't there if we do not outline some landmarks, some benchmarks in order to describe the situation. Nobody can understand the conversation without the context and this is the objective remark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, Mr. Karnavas reminded us that there was an objection to this type of question by Judge Trechsel with regard to a witness who did not have any knowledge because he had not attended the meeting. Now, Mr. Karnavas is saying that what's good for the goose a good for the gander, and he's absolutely right in saying so. Secondly, Mr. Kovacic raises other issues. He says that there was a meeting between Mr. Tudjman and representatives from Bosnia and Herzegovina, that the witness did not attend that meeting so how could he be knowledgeable about the situation, about the context? And if he's asked to comment on a situation that he has no control over, it might well be that it is the wrong opinion. Also, based on this presidential transcript that was used by Judge Prandler when he put his question to the witness, the question dealt with part of a paragraph. Now, I don't know what topic you want to address. Now, if we want to avoid this type of problem, it would have been preferable for you to say this during the examination in chief, this topic was addressed. Secondly, this topic is found again in paragraph so and so of this transcript. Then you could have asked the witness, based on his previous answer, whether he stuck to his opinion, whether he changed his mind, or whether he was speaking to another topic. You've got to, indeed, lay the foundations and we do not know what you are trying to get at as part of your cross-examination, which topics you want to raise. So please proceed, we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thanks -- thank you, Mr. President. Just for the record, I haven't asked any questions about the transcript yet I appreciate everyone's guidance. Perhaps it's a good time for the break before I begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we're going to have a break so you have 20 minutes to think it over, to prepare your question. We shall resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. For everyone's information, we've also put this transcript, we've got several of them loaded into the sanction programme and so our case manager Ms. Winner here is going to be putting the relevant pages up on the screen in sanction to assist us in following.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, this is the transcript that Judge Prandler took you to yesterday and I want to ask you just a few questions about it and then I'm going to ask you if you want to finish the answer that you wanted to finish to the question from Judge Prandler yesterday. Directing your attention to page 21 of the transcript, this is the part you looked at yesterday, I believe.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The page -- in this binder, when I say page 21, that should correspond also to the --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] That's English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also it should correspond in both languages, the page numbering should be the same.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] 21.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 21, now, based on what you've told us already, to the extent that this item refers to the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, and the taking of a historic decision to establish the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which serves as a legal basis for entry of these territories into the Republic of Croatia, if that was an objective of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, I take it you were not aware of that, you did not know that. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that at the time because I wasn't dealing with these matters, but I am aware of what's contained in this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then a similar question of item three here, to the extent that the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna recognises the full legitimacy of Dr. Franjo Tudjman as president of the Republic of Croatia and president of the HDZ, recognises his legitimacy to promote the interests of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosnia among both international factors and et cetera, you can read it there, if that was their position, if the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna recognised the full legitimacy of Franjo Tudjman to do these things on its behalf, I take it you were not aware of that, you did not know.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that there was a tendency in that direction espoused by a group of individuals, we can see the list of individuals there who made their proposal. Now, whether the president of the Republic of Croatia accepted that proposal or not is quite a different matter. He did not accept that. I can tell you right away why not, because I spoke to President Tudjman about this issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me -- I want to move on and I don't want to cut you off. As I've indicated, you can address Judge Prandler's question and add whatever you like, but I'd like to move through the document so that we can get to that point. If you could go to page 25, item 15. And again, this is the same documents which are a reflection of the minutes of the meeting of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Now, in item 15, this is calling upon "Our deputies to the Bosnia-Herzegovina assembly from the territory of Herceg-Bosna should follow instructions issued by Herceg-Bosna." Now my question there is were you aware sir or did you know that the Herceg-Bosna leadership were asserting the authority to issue instructions to the deputies who were members of the Bosnia-Herzegovina assembly at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that until this moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if I could take you to page 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I do object in the question. I didn't object earlier, as far as asserting authority. This is an aspirational document, it is suggested now they are imposing their authority I think is two different things. I just mention that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 33 there is a reference here to a statement that's being made by President Tudjman. What he's doing, he's referencing here to and I'll just read parts of it: "And to create a statelet therefore out of the remaining part around Sarajevo which mostly Muslims and some Croat Catholics would stay which would resemble the small historical land of Bosnia. It would therefore be a buffer zone in the demarcation of Serbia and Croatia and in such conditions, it would have to rely on Croatia to a large extent." Then continuing to the next paragraph. "From that viewpoint, not even some cantonization with the continuing existence of Bosnia and Herzegovina would mean for us the solution, which is the solution of demarcation." Then continuing to the next page, he says ...

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the next page, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 34. "It seems to me," feel free to follow along either on the paper or on the screen, "It seems to me, therefore, that just as we have taken advantage of this historic moment to establish an independent, internationally recognised Croatia, I believe that it is time that we take the opportunity to gather the Croatian people inside the widest possible borders." And just to finish that off, if you could go to page 106, just to stay with that thought.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you not have that in the Bosnian? It should be on the screen.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And this is during a discussion between President Tudjman and Mr. Stjepan Kljuc who, at the time, was the leader of the HDZ party in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And the president says, "Kljuc let us not waste time. We think not only I, the Croatian leadership in general thinks that since becoming head of the HDZ, you have all in all done a good job. I shall tell you, though, I shall repeat what I just said, that lately you have become closer to Izetbegovic's policy regarding those negotiations which we wanted. I have written down somewhere the date when we discussed how talks should be held with both sides, and our aim, our aim from the beginning, from the proclamation we issued, if you want, was not to preserve Bosnia and Herzegovina as it is today. Essentially, this is not in the interests of Croatian policy, as Croatian policy would in this way be permanently frustrated by the demographic and territorial loss in Bosnia and Herzegovina." "Therefore, we finally wanted and it was no accident that in the preamble to the Croatian constitution, we also mentioned the banovina of Croatia." So Mr. Ambassador, having read those portions to you, recognising that you were not present, isn't it possible that in fact based on these discussions, President Tudjman's policy at least as of this time was in fact to restore the banovina regions of Bosnia-Herzegovina and to make those Croat regions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection, calls for speculation. Isn't it possible? Anything is possible, first of all. Also we need to put it into context what is happening to the negotiations that are going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President I object to the putting the answer into the witness's mouth. That's what's happening here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Nobody's putting any answers. There was an objection by Mr. Kovacic. He wanted the context, the context in which this is being held.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We all know the context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The witness doesn't know the context. That's the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I think the witness knows very well the context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He wasn't in situ that's the whole point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The witness was the minister of the diaspora for Croatia at this time. Again, I think we're suggesting through objections answers. It's a fair question, Mr. President. If this is what's being said, did the witness know? Did this witness know if in fact this was the policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, here we go. This is the policy. My objection is this. He's being asked was this possible? Anything is possible at the time it was possible that Bosnia-Herzegovina was going to split. There were negotiations ongoing. So if we're going to be fair to this gentleman, let's talk about all the negotiations, let's talk about Izetbegovic's plan, what he was doing, while vis-a-vis working with Milosevic because only in that context can he answer this question. He wants to introduce this word "policy" because that's part of their theory of the case. We're saying in the context, in the moment, at that period of time. And we must recall that at that point, Bosnia-Herzegovina has not been declared independent and we need to look at the entire transcript that would suggest that this question, the gentleman should be given the entire transcript to read the entire transcript and only then to comment on these questions. It's unfair, it's out of context.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, recently, you complained because you were not given enough time to ask additional questions. Your demonstration is the best possible demonstration, it's something you should have done as part of your redirect. The Prosecution is putting a question to the witness. The witness gives an answer. If you don't like that answer, then you can deal with that in redirect. All the time spent on raising objections is time that comes off the time for re-examination. Of course you don't like that answer but now you are testifying in -- on behalf of the witness. You are testifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Make a couple of things clear because you are fundamentally flawed in your logic that redirect is based on whether we have sufficient time or not. That is not the basis, that's not the adversarial system, that is not the practice in any other court. And I dare say that after all these years, I'm rather shocked that this is the policy that has been adopted in this Trial Chamber with respect to my defence. Not with the Prosecution, but my Defence. That's first and foremost. Secondly, when you limit my time as you have, I ask for, I ask for some 150 or 60 hours, when I only have a certain amount of time to do a direct examination, and then you give me this answer well I should have done this on my direct well then give me the time but you're asking me to waive one right of the accused in order to benefit of the other. That is fundamentally flawed and unfair and what I'm saying in this particular instance, I have no objection to that question. However, it needs to be put into context. You indicated based on what Mr. Kovacic had raised that we need some context. This -- you're taking one sliver out of this entire event and he's being asked: Is this a possibility? And then he injected the word policy. Well let's put it into context. Let's look at the entire events, let's look at what is the conclusion of this but let's give the gentleman an opportunity to be fair and -- let's get to the truth. I can cherry pick all day long. That's not the position that we've taken. And we've asked based on what Mr. Kovacic said, we want it in context. Let's put it in context in the historical context and in the context in which this discussion was being held. And I object to the word "policy." That's something for you to decide not for the Prosecution to keep claiming that there is a policy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, if you look at the text that we are dealing with, the word "Croatian policy" comes up twice immediately after another towards the end of the first paragraph of page 106. And all Mr. Stringer was doing was asking the witness: Did he know about this, that this was held by Mr. Tudjman and he can say yes or no, but the Chamber is very well aware that this is an excerpt and a single aspect and it will -- it will evaluate this in as much context as we get and we have a lot of time or -- and I think there was no question now of in any way reducing the time for redirect. So I think Mr. Stringer you will best continue now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, particularly with this transcript, we really will have a problem if I may switch to Croatian language, sorry. [Interpretation] So far, based on the standards for the admission of evidence you introduced, we have admitted -- we have had admitted pieces of evidence numbering 1 to 2 pages which came from the presidential transcripts. Now, specifically speaking of this particular transcript we have before us, 1 to 2 pages of it will be admitted into evidence, I'm speaking of this particular transcript which relates to the meeting of the 27th of December, 1991. It has to be read throughout and none of the facts contained in the transcript can be used for the purpose of, of course, establishing the fact which is what you do as the Trial Chamber, without having read the entire transcript from page 1 to the last page. Only then can one really gain the full picture of what the meeting was all about once you've read everything, you will be able to see that this was a brainstorming session as is normally said in the western world. Now, the Prosecutor is, as my learned friend put it, cherry- picking certain segments out of this brainstorming session and on the basis of this, it will be suggested to you, Your Honours, to render a decision on the basis of that. This is just one out of the numerous such instances and this is a crucially important one. I can tell you that all of us here have been involved in the case for so long, even during the pre-trial stage and we are thoroughly familiar with the transcript and we all know that it is -- its implications are not what is being portrayed here. It is not about the policy of Croatia back in 1991. We claim that it is not and you will not be able to realise whether it is the case or not because you will only be admitting two or three pages of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, I fully agree with you. The only thing I wanted to say is this: The Prosecution or the Prosecutor is putting his case. He puts a question, the witness answers that question. All right. As far as you are concerned, as part of your cross-examination or as part of the presentation of your own case, through your own witness, you will be in a position to come back to that question and tell the witness, this witness or another witness, "Well the Prosecution asks such and such a question and receives such and such answer but wasn't this taken out of context? Isn't this portion of the transcript taken out of the context of the whole meeting?" I think that's the proper way to proceed rather than get on your feet and start shouting objections because what some of you not all of you but what some of you seem to forget is that you're dealing with professional judges and for the past two years, we've been working on this case. We -- it's something that's on our mind 24/7. The Prosecutor is doing his job as he sees fit. He receives an answer that may suit you or not, but if you believe that some information has not been provided to the Bench, then you will be free to provide this information but you do not need to do so to raise objections. You will have the opportunity to do it later. Here, we are working in an adversarial system: One of the parties puts his case, the other one its own case, and that's the way it works. Here we are dealing with policies, the banovina is mentioned in this text, it's also mentioned in the constitution as you are well aware, and the Prosecution is entitled to put a question to the witness. We'll see what the witness says. I have no idea what he's going to say. He hasn't had time to answer, but you've already raised many objections. Let's wait and see. You never know. The witness's answer might be agreeable to you because you seem to think that the Judges are silly and won't understand what it's all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... pages of this document are to be found on the e-court so everything is in fact here. It's not just -- but Ms. Alaburic, you had another point.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. I don't have an objection to raise against Mr. Stringer's question. I would like to draw your attention to one issue. I believe that the question contains a premise that needs to be clarified. The question relates to and I will be quoting a part of the transcript, to Bosnia and Herzegovina as it is today. I believe it would be very helpful to see what Bosnia-Herzegovina was like in the month of December of 1991 because by then, Croatia and Slovenia had already declared their independence, I belive that it is important to define this before the witness is allowed to answer the question because then there will be no misunderstanding upon hearing the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, you are absolutely right. Thank you for your comment. But we are professional judges and of course we've identified this problem and of course we know that at the time, Bosnia and Herzegovina was not a member of the United Nations. Of course I'm aware of that. You are dealing here with Judges who are well aware of all these facts. The Prosecutor may have given that additional piece of information but he may have assumed that we were aware of the situation in December 1991. He knew that we were knowledgeable about this. Now, taking into account the various interventions by Mr. Karnavas, Ms. Alaburic, Mr. Kovacic, and the Judges, you may proceed, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And for the record, I think Judge Trechsel has already indicated, the entirety of this transcript is already in evidence in this case and I'm putting the Prosecution case to the witness. The word "policy" is an extensive aspect of this witness's direct examination. The word "policy" is an extensive part of this conversation. I recognise that the witness wasn't present, but if things are being said and things are being done that the witness does not know about, then that bears on his views in terms of what the policy was or was not and that's what this is about, Mr. President. I hope that it's clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect, Mr. Ambassador, I am putting to you our case that there were features of Croatian policy that you were not aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Sorry for interrupting you, Mr. Stringer, but this morning, I myself put a number of questions to the witness. I asked him if there were minutes taken at these meetings. As you can see, I had anticipated this issue and we received an answer from the witness. I could also have asked him what happened when the president of a republic received people from overseas. My colleague doesn't seem to understand what I'm saying so I'm going to repeat. In such cases, would there be press statement stating that Mr. Tudjman has met X or Y and would there be reports in the press after these meetings? And at the time, were you made aware of such meetings, Witness? Because that's the way it happens everywhere in the world when President Chavez meets X or Y, I suppose that you will have reports in the press stating that Mr. Chavez met such and such person. So at the time, in December 1991, were there reports about this in the press and can we assume that anybody reading the newspapers or you yourself would have been made aware of what had happened? Yes, my fellow Judge wants to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think we should not continue interrupting. This is a phase where the Prosecutor carries out its cross-examination and we should let him do his job. Mr. Stringer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
