utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the witness to answer my question, a very technical question that has nothing to do with the cross-examination. My question is: Witness, when President Tudjman would meet someone, was -- were there minutes taken? It's a very straightforward question that can be put in relation to this particular document but that -- to any document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Minutes were taken of government meetings. Now, I don't know whether minutes were made of the meetings where Tudjman was present. As far as I know, the transcripts are the result of some tape recordings that were then transcribed. What I can tell you is that there existed official minutes made of government meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not an answer to my question. Yes, you're talking about government -- the government, but what I'm interested in is what happened when the president would meet other people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, I'm not quite sure because that was the decision taken by the president himself, whether there existed records of meetings or not when the transcripts were made or better said, when the recordings were made, I noticed that there were exchanges at the meeting. I didn't realise that there was anyone there taking notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Stringer, this has now been clarified. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, it's been a while since we've spoken so let me go back to the passages that I was reading to you before and I'm not going to read it all again but it's President Tudjman talking about, at that time, December of 1991, at least, "... not even some sort of cantonization with a continuing existence of Bosnia-Herzegovina would mean for us the solution which is the solution of demarcation." Then he goes on and he makes reference to the banovina of 1939. "That this is not in the interests of Croatian policy as Croatian policy would in this way be permanently frustrated by the demographic and territorial loss in Bosnia and Herzegovina." And then he makes reference then to the preamble to the Croatian constitution and the bano or the banovina of 1939. So this is what I'm going to put to you and you can feel free to agree or disagree with me but this is the views that we want your evidence on. Is it true that President Tudjman was at this time discussing the possibility of restoring the banovina from 1939 which was lost during World War II and doing so in order to accomplish a demarcation of -- territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and to make that territory part of a Greater Croatia or banovina as that territory was set out from 1939?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing of what you just stated is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well let's break it down then. Because we talked about President Tudjman's book of 1991 in which he discussed the unnatural aspect of Bosnia-Herzegovina in relation to Croatia. And in his book he also made a reference to the banovina. So isn't it true, then, that the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina for whatever reason, in his view, favoured restoration of the banovina as something that would be in the interests of the Croatian state. Do you disagree with me on that, restoration of the banovina would not have been in the Croatian state interest?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I definitely disagree. The Croatian banovina is a fact of the past. I have not been referring to the Croatian banovina, you have. Tudjman has never talked to me about the Croatian banovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday in your testimony, I believe you said that the territory of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna had no borders; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that in the decree on the proclamation of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, they identified a number of municipalities within Bosnia-Herzegovina that were to serve as the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The founding document of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna mentions the areas where Croats were present. It doesn't mention any borders or municipalities, for that matter. You had municipalities where Croats were in a minority or in a majority or where there was a half-half situation. The situation was quite unclear, particularly in Bosnia where there was mixed population as opposed to Herzegovina where there was a large area populated by Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in your view, then, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna did not extend to borders or municipalities per se?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On the contrary, there were attempts, as I said yesterday, there were attempts to change the borders of certain municipalities in order to make it easier for these people in order not to put one group in a subordinate position vis-a-vis the other group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we move on now, I promised that we'd give you time to answer Judge Prandler's question and so if you want to do that now, feel free to do so. My only request, Mr. President, is if that time could be assigned to the Trial Chamber and not to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're absolutely right, Mr. Stringer. One a Judge puts a question, the answer given is not taken from the time given to the party which is why sometimes Judges don't put questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to finish my answer to Your Honours. The question was asked by one of the Judges about this document. I would like to slightly correct what I said yesterday because now it turns out that in a certain way I had something against Mr. Kotroman. I was thinking about it overnight and I recalled that I had met him, but I never had any particular discussions with him; however, one of the Judges has warned me that this was not only the issue pertaining to Mr. Kotroman but to an entire group of people who wanted to see the unification of one part of Bosnia-Herzegovina with Croatia. Yesterday, I mentioned that there were such aspirations and there are such aspirations everywhere. For example, the Hungarians in Slovakia, some of them would like to unify with Hungary. Also, the Hungarians living in Subotica would like to be unified with Hungary. The Serbs wish to be unified with Republika Srpska. Therefore there are such aspiration and one such aspiration was expressed in this document when these gentlemen expressed their wish that after many centuries, they become again part of the Croatia as was the case in the Middle Ages and they thought that would be a good idea to have this part of Bosnia-Herzegovina; however, they could not be very accurate precisely because the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna did not have borders, as I said and as it is very clearly established on the document on the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. I discussed this issue with President Tudjman. The gentleman from the Defence team mentioned, and I confirmed that I did have a few meetings with President Tudjman at the time referred to by the Prosecutor Stringer why was Tudjman opposed to the wishes of these people? I will tell you now exactly what my discussion with President Tudjman was regarding these wishes. Number one, the Badinter Commission and let us not forget that this commission was part of the mediation body that was acting on behalf of the EU or rather European community at that time, and that refers to not changing the borders.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise for accounting you off and if the Trial Chamber wishes for you to continue, obviously you will be asked to do that. I'm just mentioning now that my intention is actually to go to some of the international agreements because you're starting to refer to international agreements or negotiations such as the Badinter Commission. So my proposal, if the Trial Chamber agrees is to move to the joint statement of April 1993 rather than continue with, I think what is possibly becoming a bit of an unwieldy --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the second time Mr. Stringer cut off the witness. I don't mean to object but I believe he was answering the Judge's question. Now if the Judge wishes to cut the gentleman off, then it's up to the Judge. He may be satisfied with the answer but I believe that the gentleman is entitled to provide a complete answer. He's trying -- he's attempting to answer completely and I think we should allow the witness to fully answer the question. I realise that we have time constraints but I think out of respect we should listen to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Stringer. Mr. Karnavas has just said that when a question is put by a Judge, well, the witness answers the question. I feel that he answers the question controlled by the Judge putting the question. I won't interfere. When a Judge raises an issue it's not for me to say whether it's a good or bad question, I don't have anything to say even if I don't understand the questions at the times, but the witness answers based on the Judge's question. If you now intervene, this might be detrimental to the question in it's completeness. From what I understand, maybe I'm wrong but the witness wanted to give more details about Mr. Kostroman compared to yesterday. That's what I understood. I think it's best for him to finish and then you can go back to the international agreements because you want to review them with him. But Judge Prandler is the one controlling matters here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm of course aware of the time factor and the time constraints as was mentioned by Mr. Karnavas, that is number one. Number two that yesterday when I asked the question, I prefaced my question with the acknowledgment that of course the witness was not there at that meeting which was when the issues were discussed according to the presidential transcript. So my question was the following: The -- since we spoke about the citizenship and we spoke about the relevant provisions of the constitution of the Republic of Croatia and we spoke about the situation of the naturalization and which gave very wide latitude as far as the legislation is concerned to recognise as Croats all those in the diaspora and elsewhere therefore I asked if that very transcript where Mr. Ignac Kostroman as secretary of the HDZ at that time, when he reported about the decisions taken by the governing board to put it simply of the HDZ, all those relevant issues which you have there on page 21 of -- 21 of the transcript, they are item 1, position to item 2, item 3, et cetera, my question was if the witness, if Ambassador Sancevic sees any linkage, a link of those issues which are -- which have been discussed there and raised there as well as the issues which were related to the citizenship. In other words, somehow I believe that was a euphoria among the Croats at that time that they belonged to the same nation, they have to be treated, let's say it is my view at least or it is my impression that like in Herceg-Bosna as well that now it was a historical moment when their aspirations could be satisfied. Both in terms of nationality, citizenship, and as far as the territorial arrangements are concerned. It was my impression that that is why I asked the question if there was any linkage, any kind of joint common views expressed from the official circles of Croatia at that time, that is President Tudjman and the government as well as the participants of the HDZ leadership in Herceg-Bosna. So my question is if the witness, if Ambassador Sancevic believes that it was correct, my impression correct that there was certain linkage, certain cooperation between the two parts of - let me put it this way - of the Croatian nation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can give you a specific answer to your question. Before this transcript, the Badinter Commission had established that no frontier can be changed in the eastern or southeastern Europe, period. That was accepted by President Tudjman and that is what we discussed. Therefore, it was an obligation to abide by Badinter's decisions. There can be no change of borders. Therefore, this wish, unfortunately, expressed by these gentlemen could not be fulfilled. The second reason is you know that there was a Serbian so-called republic in Croatia. If the gentleman from Bosnia-Herzegovina would join Croatia, then the gentleman from the Serbian Republic of Krajina could easily join Serbia. Therefore, that was the second argument against Tudjman's acceptance or even giving any thought to any unification between Herceg-Bosna and Croatia. There's another reason pertaining to this issue. From the very beginning, since there could be no change of borders and since consequently there could be no joining or unification between any parties, and since the chief argument of the state of Croatia was that there could be no cessation of the republic of Serbian Krajina from Croatia equally, there could be no unification between the republics -- sorry not to the republic but rather the Community of Herceg-Bosna and Croatia. Ever since then but even before that time when the Badinter Commission had taken these decisions, the policy pursued by President Tudjman, i.e., the Croatian state policy towards Bosnia and Herzegovina was to preserve Bosnia and Herzegovina definitely as a friendly state, et cetera. Because there was another thing. If the greater Serbs managed to divide Bosnia-Herzegovina then we would have the state of Serbia about 100 kilometres away from Zagreb. That was the third argument put forward by President Tudjman and in my talks with him, why the proposal made by people who wanted to see the unification could not have been accepted. From that point on, both President Tudjman and his government and myself as the ambassador and the representative of the Croatian government implementing the Croatian state policy towards Bosnia and Herzegovina, we were all in favour of Bosnia and Herzegovina because we saw it as the only solution, and we managed to persuade and to convince the gentlemen who had wanted unification with Croatia that this would not be in anyone's interest and that our official policy was -- meaning the policy of the Croatian government and the Croatian state, was the preservation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the protection of the Croatian communities according to the constitution within Bosnia and Herzegovina. Hence, this permanent aspect -- Tudjman tried to persuade these people by telling them: This is very well, gentlemen, that you wish to see this that you are deriving arguments from the past but you have to face the reality. You have to face the facts. Therefore, there can be no possibility for this to become a reality. And President Tudjman managed to convince the people around him. And I persuaded everybody else in Bosnia and Herzegovina that we had to abide by the policy laid down by the Badinter's Commission and to see which will be -- and to see that that will be most beneficial for Croatia. I don't know if I was too explicit in my answer but if you need any further details, please do ask me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ambassador Sancevic. Let me also say that I have been interested in the issues and I appreciate your answer because of the fact that personally, I am very much interested as a Hungarian as you may know and since you referred to instances when Hungarians around the present Hungary, I was also interested in certain better solutions than exist nowadays and that is why I asked the question yesterday when we spoke about the nationality and the issue of the citizenship, et cetera. I appreciate your answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, then, I wanted to take you to the next exhibit which is marked as P02088, and I believe this is one that you were shown on your direct examination. It is in -- it will be in the Prosecution binder, I believe. No, I'm sorry, Defence binder 2088. This is the joint statement dated 24th of April, 1993. This was the one which makes a reference to the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. It bears the signatures of Mate Boban and Mr. Alija Izetbegovic and with President Tudjman as witnessing the document. Just to sort of set the context?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] DO5088.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry P as in Prosecution. 2088. It may be on the ELMO, on the screen I'm not sure. Yes, it's also on the screen in front of you, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will set the context here. April of 1993, you are the Croatian ambassador to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document, the joint statement actually includes your name at the beginning as a person who was part of the Croatian delegation?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in terms of the context here, April 24th, 1993, we had only about nine or ten days earlier seen some serious conflicts break out in Central Bosnia between Croats and Muslims; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between certain Croats and certain Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that there were military conflicts between the HVO and the Muslim armed forces in Central Bosnia at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, as the connoisseur of the situation, I must tell you the following: There were various war lords there. There were people who single-handedly did certain things because within these armed forces, there were elements from the former Yugoslavia, there were elements who had come from abroad, there were elements who at the time existed or were emerging as military experts or commanders. Let me just give you one example. I arrived in Croatia in 1991 as an ordinary private with the military book of the army of Venezuela but in the meantime, I became a colonel. In other words, the situation was fluctuating towards the local commander. Therefore, I am not in favour of generalisations. I don't like to hear when somebody says that the BH army was in conflict with the HVO. That was not the case everywhere, but where did these things happen? These things happened where you had extremists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well let me try to be more specific on that because I think the background here, there is a reason why this joint statement is being issued, and I believe it has to do with the fact that the members of the HVO units attached to the Central Bosnia Operative Zone which was based in Vitez had armed conflicts with units attached to the 3rd Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Would you agree with me on that point?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree, but I wouldn't say all of them because even in Central Bosnia, there were units that were not in conflict with each other. Only the units that were run or under the supervision of extremists were the ones who entered conflicts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I mentioned Vitez in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone now, do you know if that Central Bosnia Operative Zone was under the command of a Mr. Tihomir Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you are now taking me to the territory which is -- with which I am not familiar with. I was not involved in the Defence. I was a political representative. I was an ambassador. Therefore, now you're asking me a question I don't know who started when and who the commander was. I had the general idea of what was going on, but it's really absurd for me to go into details. It is true that I did make the maps made by Mr. Praljak, but you will not find in those maps the names of the commanders because that was not within my purview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just said that the connoisseur of the situation, that was the word that was given to me in English.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Could you repeat? Could you repeat?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had indicated that you were the connoisseur and so I thought you were the ...

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of the general situation, but I never got involved in military matters because I didn't want to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could I get an interpretation of the last ...

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I think that was a right thing to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One follow-up question. Witness, you answered the question but I think there's something missing. You were the ambassador. Normally speaking, you had a load of information coming to you. I suppose so. I don't know. If something happened in Bosnia and Herzegovina, something reported by the international media, would Mr. Granic or the Ministry of Foreign Affairs call you to ask you to send a report, a telegram on the said event? Did that sort of thing happen or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it did happen that I regularly sent my reports. They were very modest, very reduced because I at one point realised that my diplomatic mail was being checked and that's when I reduced my reports to five sentences, to a piece of paper, and the only thing that you could see there was President Tudjman and Minister of Foreign Affairs Mate Granic, three lines, five lines, that was all. What mattered was the synthesis of the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. In my reports, I never ever mentioned any details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So -- and that's just in context. The joint statement, then, is being issued in the wake of a fairly serious military conflict that had taken place in Central Bosnia; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we have Lord Owen is directly involved in this joint statement. I take it, then, that there was fairly intense international pressure on the HVO or the Bosnian Croats, if you will, and the Bosnian Muslims to reach some sort of an agreement to diffuse the situation. Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree that that was the goal of one part of the international community. There was no complete consensus on the part of the international community. I can tell you that some even showed that they were in favour of the Greater Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know, I think you might be referring to something that we read in your book. I know that you've written in your book, and you've been fairly critical of certain members of the international community along the lines that you've just mentioned, that is, that certain powers in the international realm, in fact, favoured, in your view, a conflict between the Croats and Muslims because that would enhance or would facilitate the Greater Serbia. Is that your view?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I wrote, and I'm here to tell the truth and nothing but the truth, and I adhere by that truth. What I wrote has been written and that is why at least in my book, I have evidence for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me take a few moments to explore that with you, Mr. Ambassador while we're on it. I'm going to jump ahead in my outline so it's going to take me just a moment to find the document. Well, let me just come back to it because I'm not ready to go there and I don't want to take more time. Yesterday Judge Trechsel in the context of this and the Medjurgorje Agreement that followed on the 18th of May, Judge Trechsel asked whether, in your view, the parties had an equal attitude in respect of these agreements. I believe that's the word he used. I would like to explore with you, since you were a party to these negotiations, in any event, whether, in fact, there was disagreement on the Croatian side and the Muslim side about what these various agreements actually meant and how they would be implemented. So now if you could set aside that document which is the joint declaration, I'd like to take you to another one of the presidential transcripts that's marked as P02059 and this one we have in sanction as well so if the usher can help you get the document, Mr. Ambassador, we can also put the transcript on the screen for you. P02059 and this will be in the Prosecution binders. This is an interesting one, Mr. Ambassador, and again I recognise it's not one where it appears you were present - I could be wrong - but it's a transcript of a meeting that occurred that same night of 24 April 1993 just before this joint declaration was issued because if you go back to the joint declaration, and you don't have to do it but on the second page -- or I'm sorry, the final page, you see that it was actually issued on the 25th of April, 1993 at quarter before 1.00 in the morning. Now, this transcript is in fact the transcript of a meeting with Tudjman, Mr. Izetbegovic, and also Lord Owen and this is actually the transcript of the discussion that precedes the issuance of that joint declaration. So getting back to the question, the interpretation of the parties and whether the parties shared the same views, there are some comments and there are some remarks in here that are made that I would like to direct you to and see if you can comment on that. That starts on page -- I'm sorry, page 11 of the transcript which will be the same in both languages because this is early in the meeting and each of the parties makes sort of an opening presentation. These are some of the things that President Izetbegovic says. I'm going to move now actually to page 12, which is the next page. This is what he says, they're talking about the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. "Our impression is that the HVO and the Republic of Croatia do not want the Vance-Owen Plan as it stands." This is Izetbegovic talking. He says, "First of all, we accepted this plan because we thought that Bosnia and Herzegovina could not contain some exclusively ethnic and national territories because it is a mixed country." Then he says, skipping one line, "Judging by the HVO actions, they understood this plan in a completely different manner. Despite the fact that, under the mediation of Mr. Vance and Mr. Owen, we have signed a document, an agreement, whose first item explicitly says that the provinces are not national territories of any one of the peoples who cannot lay claim to it only for themselves. If we have signed this ..." he says. Then skipping down a couple of lines, he says, "In other words, Herceg-Bosna as a state entity, as a type of state entity, could not exist after the signing of the Vance-Owen Plan." Then the next line he says that, "During talks with Mr. Owen, I heard several times that this was only a temporary solution until the problem in Bosnia and Herzegovina was solved, that Herceg-Bosna was a temporary solution until some other solution was found." So I've got some more passages but just based on that, this is my question: You testified yesterday that Mr. Izetbegovic unreservedly signed the Vance-Owen Peace Plan and my question to you is whether, in fact, he had strong reservations and those were the kinds of reservations that he's expressing here about the way in which the Vance-Owen Peace Plan is being interpreted by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, as far as the Vance-Owen Plan is concerned, the Republic of Croatia gave its full support to the original text of the plan irrespective of whether it was about the constitutional organisation or the internal division. In other words, if the final text of the Vance-Owen Plan had been accepted as it was proposed, the division would have been the same as was proposed by Mr. Vance and Mr. Owen. Mr. Izetbegovic and his associates accepted gladly the aspects of the constitutional organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina but they did not agree with the provinces or the internal division as it was envisaged. However, at one point, Mr. Izetbegovic signed every single thing and then later on, he had second thoughts especially with regard to the geographical division and he was against that so that at one point, not only the Greater Serbs never accepted the Vance-Owen Plan, but also Izetbegovic had his objections to the Vance-Owen Plan. Croatia, on the other hand, never had any objections but rather gave its full support to the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Setting aside Croatia, the Republic of Croatia, let's talk about the HVO and the Herceg-Bosna people and their interpretation of the Vance-Owen Plan because that's what I think President Izetbegovic is referring to here and he's reporting this to President Tudjman and as someone who was involved in the various discussions and negotiations, would you agree with me that these were problems that Mr. Izetbegovic was expressing that, in fact, there were problems with the way that the HVO was implementing the Vance-Owen Plan, that there were disagreements about what the plan means and how it should be implemented and that was really the cause of the problems at this time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, their situations with regard to the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan were they could not agree. But when Mr. Izetbegovic put his signature on the Vance-Owen Plan, he accepted it at that moment. Later on, he gave up on the plan and that was the reason and the situation which led to the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan which was an amendment to the original plan and the second plan was the so-called union of the republics. I would also like to mention that Mr. Izetbegovic, whom I knew very well and had frequent exchanges of thoughts with him and I could even say this, we were friends. Mr. Izetbegovic was always occupied with the unitarian Bosnia and Herzegovina and all the plans of the international community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will ask you about the unitarian Bosnia and Herzegovina so as I take it I'm looking at the transcript, with regard to the implementation of Vance-Owen it appears to me you were saying there were situations with regard to the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan where they could not agree, the parties had differences about how the plan should be implemented; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be very specific, there were problems with regard to the command post in Central Bosnia. There were disagreements as to where the Croatian HVO commander was supposed to be, in which province, and also where the commander of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was supposed to be located. And there was a bit of a tug of war with regard to who is going to be the boss of all bosses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just continue with another passage. Page 15 where Izetbegovic is saying: "There would have been no conflict if Mr. Boban, instead of sending troops to Travnik or to Vitez, had called on Mostar residents to organise and participate with him in government in accordance with the Vance-Owen Plan. There would have been no conflict had they called on Muslims to participate in government, as envisaged by the Vance-Owen Plan, if this had been the first step. They would have been more than happy to accept, because a large number of people do not participate in government, professors do not want to hold classes, judges do not want to go to courts, policemen do not want to join in, because everywhere they are told they have to accept and write an application to Herceg-Bosna, and they want to establish a Mostar province." He says, "We have accepted the Mostar province, but we have not accepted the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. We have accepted the Vance-Owen Plan, because it envisages provinces and does not envisage a Croatian Herceg-Bosna, because Mostar is not and will never be only Croatian. You can terrorise Mostar for years but you will never rule over it." "So we can govern there jointly. Mostar cannot be governed only by the Croatian people." That's what Izetbegovic is saying on the night of the 24th of April. Now, this, again, gets into interpretation of the Vance-Owen and my question based on this one is whether, on the Croat side, the HVO side, whether the HVO or Herceg-Bosna interpretation was that in certain provinces under Vance-Owen, the Croats would govern exclusively and that what Izetbegovic is saying here is that he does not accept that view, they want to govern jointly in Mostar. Is that basically the problem here, the conflict. The Croats have a view of territorial exclusivity in terms of governance whereas the Muslims see something has more joint in these territories under the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, the reflection of the Vance-Owen Plan can be found on the 18th of August 1993 when people were elected in various provinces and they all agreed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As of this time, I'm asking now about August -- I'm sorry, April 1993, at this time -- right -- there were disagreements on two sides and I'm not even asking you to take a side. I'm simply asking you as someone who was involved, isn't it true that the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats had strongly different opinions and views in terms of how the Vance-Owen Plan should be implemented on the ground?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't agree with you. You keep on generalising things. Bosnian-Herzegovinian Croats, Bosnian-Herzegovinian Muslims. Some Bosnian-Herzegovinian Croats and some Bosnian-Herzegovinian Muslims could not agree but there were others such was Mr. Prlic and others who were always prone to agreeing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well let's talk about the individuals who signed the joint statement, that is Mr. Izetbegovic on the Muslim side and Mr. Boban on the Croat side.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The page ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This goes back to the -- this is the joint statement which is the document itself. I can just simply -- if you will accept my representation that it was signed by Mr. Boban and Mr. Izetbegovic on behalf of those two and what I'm asking is in terms of the Izetbegovic faction and the Boban faction, there was real disagreement about how the Vance-Owen Plan was to be implement in April of 1993.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say the following: There was a period of time when they agreed with regard to the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan. Whatever Mr. Alija Izetbegovic signed, an agreement could be reached there. However, the situation was very fluid. At any given moment, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic would again revert or rather go back to his old phases of the unitarian rather than federal Republic of Croatia and then when he reverted to that, then obviously the Vance-Owen Plan started falling apart in a certain way and this finally led to Owen-Stoltenberg Plan which was an attempt to win over the Greater Serbian side and also an attempt to satisfy the Muslim side, although none of the plans gave up on the federal organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I can assure you we will go to the issue of the unitary Bosnia and Herzegovina as I've indicated, I'm not quite there yet in my outline, but we will definitely asking your views on that. I think it might be -- I'm being told we have 10 minutes, Mr. President, or is it time for the break now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise -- excuse me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ten more minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We're going to go for another ten minutes and then take a break. Is that okay with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, you say your positions. I represented the Croatian state policy vis-a-vis Bosnia and Herzegovina. Those were not my positions. Please do not use those words. Just a while ago, you said, "Let's hear your positions" what does it mean my positions? I represented the state of Croatia and I followed an official policy, the official policy of the Republic of Croatia vis-a-vis the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I must add today that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. I think I was just indicating that we're going to be asking for your testimony or your evidence on that. I recognise that you're distinguished between your personal views and your views that were expressed on behalf of the official policy but I'm just talking in general terms about your evidence and your testimony. Now, that's the joint declaration and it was issued just minutes after this discussion that we've been referring to. In the next event, the next big event, if you will, actually there are a number because things are happening quickly, in May of 1993 I take it you are aware, sir, that -- on the 9th of May, 1993, then, a pretty large conflict, a fierce conflict broke out in the town of Mostar between, again, on one side forces of the HVO and forces of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the other.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. That was the 9th, 10th of May and then you move forward about nine days, then, to the 18th of May which is the Medjurgorje Agreement that I will be asking you about. But in the meantime, there was just one -- there was one document I wanted to show you to get your testimony about and that's Exhibit P09602. This is in the Prosecution binder. It might also be on the screen in front of you, Mr. Ambassador. This is a document that I expect you have not seen but as someone who was a diplomat, an ambassador, I want to ask your views about this letter. If you want to take a moment to read it, that's fine. It's called a note verbal, it's dated the 6th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see two pages and I've not read them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's called a "note verbal" it's been issued by the office of Mr. Mate Boban and you can see at the bottom of the second page it's being directed to the Secretary-General of the United Nations Security Council and other countries. If you want to take a moment to read the entire letter, you can otherwise I can just go over it with you together okay. In this letter, Mr. Boban makes a reference to a meeting, a joint session of the political bodies of the Croat people in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Presidency of the HDZ for Bosnia-Herzegovina. This joint session that was held in Citluk on the 29th of April chaired by Mr. Boban a Mr. Franjo Boras as president as well, as well as a Mr. Mile Akmadzic. Do you know those gentlemen, Mr. Boras or Mr. Akmadzic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Mr. Franjo Boras. I know Mr. Miho Lasic because he was my minister in the embassy of the Republic of Croatia and I also know Mr. Akmadzic because when Mr. Akmadzic was the prime minister, I asked for his permission to allow the Croatian troops then to Bosnia-Herzegovina and he granted that permission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that by the way?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was before the new liberation of Dubrovnik, President Tudjman had informed me that -- the coastal area around Dubrovnik would be returned. Dubrovnik was, at the time, besieged and the Croatian troops were on their way to liberate Dubrovnik. I wrote a letter to Mr. Akmadzic who, at the time, was the prime minister of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I asked for his permission for the Croatian troops to be allowed to enter a part of Herzegovina because in that narrow area of the former Dubrovnik republic, it was absolutely impossible to realize or carry out some military operations because the area was so small and narrow and Mr. Akmadzic in agreement with Mr. Izetbegovic granted us permission for Croatian troops to be allowed to enter the territory of Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Lasic, when was he the minister in the Croatian embassy? Do you know what period of time he was there? You said he was your minister, I believe.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what period of time did he act?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the moment when I left for Sarajevo after the Washington Accords, I opened an embassy which was much bigger than the one in Medjurgorje because this was a very big and major embassy that was to work on the implementation of the Washington Accords. I needed an assistant. I needed somebody who was familiar with the situation in Sarajevo and so on and so forth, and I asked for Mr. Miho Lasic to be assigned to the embassy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just getting back to this letter which is the Boban "note verbal" that went to the UN Secretary -General and to the others, what this is is sort of an announcement that after consideration these following conclusions were decided and announced. What this says is that the legitimate and legal representatives of the Croat people in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, number one, they deny -- do you see paragraph one there?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That the legitimate and legal representatives of the Croat people in Bosnia and Herzegovina: "Deny legal validity of all decisions of the Presidency and government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina rendered without the participation of the elected representatives of the Croat people." This is number two, "Deny legitimacy for all diplomatic and consular representatives of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina world-wide." Thirdly, "They deny legitimacy and legality to newly-elected officials from the ranks of the Croat people in bodies of the republic's government without the confirmation of the Presidency of the HDZ for Bosnia-Herzegovina." And finally, they "Deny legality of representation and legitimization of Mr. Alija Izetbegovic and in the function of the president of the Presidency of the R BiH." That Izetbegovic is considered only as a representative of the Muslims. Now, I know that you haven't seen this before but as an ambassador and someone who was a politician at the time, this coming about 12 days after the issuance of the joint declaration, right, in which the parties are going to attempt to implement together the terms of the Vance-Owen Plan and to go forward peacefully after the conflicts in Central Bosnia, it seems to me, Mr. Ambassador, that issuing a letter like this and sending it to the Secretary-General of the United Nations as well as all the embassies of the countries where Bosnia-Herzegovina has an embassy that would seem to me to be counter-productive in the extreme and would in fact hinder efforts of the parties to work together. My question is whether you agree with me whether you can comment on the impact such a letter would have in the climate that existed at the time of the joint statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me Mr. Ambassador, before we hear that, obviously there is a space in time, and I think we need to draw the attention to the gentleman with respect to paragraph number one because I think it's important to put it into context. The question is: Are there -- are there Croatian representatives -- this is the Presidency --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I'm going to object to putting the answer in the witness's mouth. This witness --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the two speakers please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's a trick question, assuming that the government --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your microphone phone is off. Mr. Karnavas's microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Assuming that the Presidency was properly functioning, I can -- I see the question as being proper but we have to look at what transpired in the meantime. If that -- if we're not dealing with a different government then obviously it calls into question the -- the legitimacy of that government and therefore, his question is improper. That's the whole point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Wouldn't the witness know this and include it in his answer? I think you're referring to the reason behind number one and the justification for it and wouldn't that be something that the witness would be perfectly able to comment on?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, if you could switch off your mike. Now, I would agree with you presumably if we had some foundation. We're presuming that the gentleman knows what was happening in Sarajevo at the time keeping in mind that this is -- this is in May. He was roving at the time. So there is some -- there are some facts that require some -- that's what -- I'm trying to be fair, I'm not trying to obstruct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Would you turn off your microphone, please. I have no other conception of your intervention. I'm sure Mr. Stringer will ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The witness -- you know, there are some witnesses who, I think, are pretty not susceptible to trick questions and my impression is that this is one. The gentleman was a Croatian ambassador to Bosnia-Herzegovina. He can read the letter. He's read the letter. He knows what the situation was in Sarajevo at the time. I've asked him, in his capacity as a diplomat, what impact, if any, such language like this would have on the parties' attempts at reconciliation. I think it's a fair question and I expect that he will take into account the context at the time that the letter was written.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to underline once again that my relationships were with the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I never interfered with the internal affairs of Bosnia and Herzegovina but as far as concerned Mr. Boban and what he writes, these are his ideas. I had nothing whatsoever to do with them, I'm not defending them, I'm not attacking them. Mr. Boban wrote what he did and it's a fact. I do not wish to provide any comment on something that I wasn't involved in, that I did not have a specific insight into. I said, didn't I, that I had contact with Mr. Boban only once, that I visited him only once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to have a break, a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, I believe you want to seek clarification regarding filings and Mr. Kovacic too. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I asked for two minutes only and my learned friend agreed. The Praljak Defence made a filing called Slobodan Praljak's notice regarding his intent to tender 1D AA statement pursuant to Rule 92 ter yesterday afternoon. [In English] like one hour ago and we discovered that there was one error inadvertently, pages from 42304 were added to that submission -- this material and those pages starting with 42304 up to the last page which is 42292 are actually not needed in that submission. We will file in writing that corrigendum during the afternoon; however, I wanted that the other parties which might read that saving their time. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador the last round of questions had to do with the period of April 1993 and the issuance of the joint statement on the 24th. The next sort of topic or time frame I'd like to ask you about is the period of the Medjurgorje Agreement that was dated the 18th of May 1993 and again just to set the context in the sense of the Medjurgorje agreement, you indicated I think just before the break that you were aware of a strong conflict that broke out in Mostar on the 9th of May between the HV [sic] and the Armija Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that. I said that a conflict broke out between some units of the BH army and some units of the HVO, not all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The record indicates page 76, line 13, if I said HV, I meant to say HVO. Where were you when the conflict broke out in Mostar on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a roving ambassador at the time based in Neum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are you saying it's likely that you were in Neum or that -- can you tell us? Do you recall where you were? If you don't recall, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was either in Neum where the Mostar University was housed in the same hotel or I was on one of my travels in the free territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in other words, I never entered the territory controlled by the Greater Serbia aggressor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you at some point learn in any detail about the events that had taken place in Mostar at the time, the ABiH, for example, had headquarters in west Mostar that was captured by the HVO. I'm just trying to get an idea of the level of your knowledge of the incident itself?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall reading about some of the events that occurred I also recall that I was on one of my travels around about that time and that I came across Mr. Prlic who, to my recollection, showed to me the process of rebuilding the bridges in Mostar. Do not forget that the Serbs had destroyed all the bridges in Mostar. Then there was an American unit there providing services free of charge, reconstructing bridges in Mostar and I recall our conversation there in Mostar. I don't think our conversation had anything to do with the conflicts themselves. We spoke only of the positive matters as to what could be done in Mostar to make it operational, to help it reconstruct the bridges and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to Mostar during those days --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During those days, the 9th, 10th or 11th of May?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I predominantly travelled in three directions. I took one route across western Herzegovina in the direction of Livno. That was one route.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry to cut you off. I'm asking you specifically about the 9th, 10th, 11th of May. Did you go to Mostar town personally during those three days at all?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I was over those three days. I'm merely telling you what it is that I remember, and I remember that roughly at the time I travelled in three directions, one toward Livno, the other one toward Central Bosnia, and the third toward Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the conversation you had with Dr. Prlic you just referred to about the bridges, was that during the first part of May or did that conversation take place at a different time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't set an exact date on that, I don't remember, but I believe it was roughly in the early days of my tenure as the roving ambassador.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So this would have been during possibly 1992 or the first part of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first part of 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, getting back to Mostar around the 9th/10th of May, did you become aware at some point that as part of the events there, a large number of Muslims from the Mostar area had been taken out and were being held at a place called the Heliodrom facility that was south of the city?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that all of us came to know about this through the New York Times. Since this was the source of information we had, I immediately conveyed the information to my superior, Mr. Granic, who in turn informed Tudjman and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, counsel on your direct examination, excuse me, he took me to the Medjurgorje Agreement and I don't need to ask you more questions about the agreement itself but like I did with the joint statement from April, I'd like to ask you a couple questions, perhaps, if you can shed light on some of the discussions and the positions that were being taken in the background during the negotiations between the parties. On that point, if you would look to a different exhibit, P02441, it's in the Prosecution binder. P02441. I think they can put it on the screen also, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this is a document that you haven't seen before, it's a UN report, a United Nations report about the meeting that occurred on the 18th of May between the parties which led to the Medjurgorje Agreement. And I know that you are not indicated here as a participant in this particular meeting, although it was my recollection from yesterday that you did participate in some of the discussions related to the Medjurgorje Agreement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Medjurgorje. I was in Split before that. All of that being within President Tudjman's action for peace. On the 18th of May, the first part of the day was spent in Split at a meeting comprising various representatives of the international community, there was the Russian foreign minister, I can't recall his name. Then there was Mr. Petersen as the ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this point, we don't need to know all the participants in the Split meeting, if you weren't there, but I just wanted to make sure that you are a person who can tell us --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you were there. You were not at the Medjurgorje meeting that's referred to in this document.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended both meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I stand corrected. Then in terms of this exhibit, 2441, on the second page, there is a reference to Mr. Petersen, who was talking and what he says is, among other things, is that on behalf of the international community, he was reiterating a strong support of the council of ministers to the Vance-Owen Plan and he alluded to the shock and dismay in Europe over recent events which had not only threatened the hopes of Bosnia but it also affected Croatia's relations with Europe. My question there, sir, is this: Isn't it true that at this time, the international view, the world view was that Croatia did bear some involvement or responsibility for the events that had taken place in Mostar during the 9th and 10th of May by virtue of its association with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In its relations toward Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia -- or let me put it this way. The views held by representatives of the international community were divided. Not all of them held the same view such as the one expressed by Mr. Petersen. It was due to Mr. Petersen's views that President Tudjman wanted to have Mr. Petersen and all the other important international players both in Split and in Medjurgorje. What was at stake was to salvage the Vance-Owen proposal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for whatever reason, there was a lot of pressure on Croatia in order to make that happen in the wake of the events in Mostar on the 9th and 10th of May.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the representatives of the international community grasped what was going on, especially the tendencies to create an Islamic Bosnia-Herzegovina and there were others who ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to cut you off but I was simply asking whether you recall whether there was a lot of pressure on Croatia in order to make the Vance-Owen Plan work. Do you recall, yes or no, whether there was pressure on Croatia to use its influence?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was pressure on Croatia but not in relation to the Vance-Owen Plan since Croatia had been supporting it all along. Aren't I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. If you'll turn the page, there's another passage I want to ask you some questions about. What's happening here on the next page of this, there's a paragraph that begins with the words, "President Izetbegovic and is says, "President Izetbegovic agreed that the political and military situations were closely related and that there was also agreement that the Vance-Owen Peace Plan be implemented." Here we're getting to this issue of implementation and what does that mean. "He suggested therefore the parties start out from where they were in agreement and recommended the formation of the provinces and their authorities be a priority, the problem of Mostar having arisen due to the denial of participation of Muslims in the local authority." Now -- and then it continues: "However, it would be necessary for Mr. Boban to publicly and clearly admit that the republic of Herceg-Bosnia no longer existed and that the formed provinces could not be considered national territories or the exclusive right of any one peoples." So on that point, I'm just trying to recapture the positions of the parties and your views on that based on your own involvement. We looked at the transcript earlier from April 24th and Mr. Izetbegovic was saying that Herceg-Bosna can't exist under Vance-Owen. And that the Vance-Owen provinces cannot be the exclusive territory of any one party. Do you recall or can you say whether, in fact, he was expressing the same views then as part of the Medjurgorje negotiations? Because it appears to me that according to this report, he's saying the same thing in May that he was saying in April.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will put it this way: In May in Medjurgorje, there existed a consensus between Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to follow the Vance-Owen Plan. Now, there were always some minor problems when it came to the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan, everybody wanted grist to their own will, and I believe that Alija Izetbegovic admitted at the time that they were in agreement, meaning him with Tudjman, that the Vance-Owen Plan had to be implemented.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, and I think we all accept that everyone was signing agreements and saying that the Vance-Owen Plan should be implemented. On that, Mr. Ambassador, we can agree. I'm trying to go behind that. Let me put it to you this way: When Izetbegovic says that under Vance-Owen, Herceg-Bosna cannot exist, was there agreement on that point?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Vance-Owen Plan envisaged provinces. The idea was that provinces should be set up and automatically, through the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan, the provinces would be set up and Herceg-Bosna, the way it, in fact, existed at the time was supposed to adjust to the newly arisen situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, under the Vance-Owen Plan, Mr. Ambassador, isn't it true that there were cantons and they were all given numbers and that the maps that the Vance-Owen Plan and the ones that were signed by Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Boban made no reference to Herceg-Bosna. Can we agree on that point? There were numbers, if you will ...

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were cantons and their numbers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And so Mr. Izetbegovic was taking the position that the Bosnian -- that the Boban faction, if you will, they had to repudiate Herceg-Bosna; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's quite clear, it was quite clearly formulated in the Vance-Owen Plan which Croatia supported and endorsed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Are you familiar, do you know, if Mr. Boban and his faction ever repudiated Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact of the matter was quite different. The Vance-Owen Plan failed -- can you allow me to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, if I could ask you to just answer my question and then you can make the point that you wanted to make, the question is: Do you know if Mr. Boban and his faction ever repudiated Herceg-Bosna? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By virtue of accepting the Vance-Owen Plan, it became inevitable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Previously, I said that what had to be done was to adapt Herceg-Bosna to the Vance-Owen Plan which ultimately fell through not because of the Muslim-Croat side but because of the Serb side which he refused to accept the plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask this part of it and this makes reference to the next few words, setting aside the words or the name Herceg-Bosna, didn't the Boban faction -- weren't they advancing a concept of Vance-Owen that was based upon territories being the exclusive right of one people? And again we see Izetbegovic is complaining about that, "... provinces could not be considered national territories or the exclusive right any one people." Didn't the Boban faction consider the Croatian territories or provinces to be national territories for themselves, that is for Croats exclusively?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, definitely not. Under the Vance-Owen Plan, the envisaged provinces were determined largely in such a way that there was one side which had a predominant majority. The Vance-Owen Plan did not provide for any exclusive provinces. I repeat that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna did not have any borders. It was the Vance-Owen Plan that determined borders in terms of provinces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One last question on this document. The next sentence regarding the Medjurgorje agreement indicates that or what Izetbegovic was saying was that, "The meeting should not end without first resolving the issue of the civilians still detained in Mostar." That's the last sentence of that paragraph. Do you recall whether 9 days after the 9th of May, that is on the 18th, Muslims were still being detained at the Heliodrom facility, for example, south of Mostar. Did you go to the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't at the Heliodrom, I was at Dretelj, with Mr. Mato Granic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was in September 1993, that was later.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever the date, I don't recall it specifically, I was with Mr. Mato Granic and the International Committee of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I've got some questions about that a little bit later. The next exhibit, Mr. Ambassador, is P -- yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Ambassador, I have a technical question to put to you. We have a transcript of the meeting of the 18th of May 1993 between President Tudjman, President Izetbegovic and Mr. Mate Boban. I reviewed very closely the list of participants to that meeting, and I couldn't find your name. I'm quite surprised to see that the ambassador of the Republic of Croatia did not attend the meeting when we see that the president of a republic is there and I also noticed that the minister in charge of foreign affairs is not present either. Do you know why you did not attend the meeting or is it so that you attended the meeting but your name, for some reason, does not appear on the list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not present at the meeting and I don't remember why. There must have been an important reason why I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, the next exhibit is P10398. It's in the Prosecution binder. While that one is being located, in your direct examination this week, you talked about various speeches that were given by President Tudjman and how they reflected the policy of the Republic of Croatia. This is a report about the speech that President Tudjman gave in Siroki Brijeg on the 20th of May, 1993, two days after the Medjurgorje Agreement. As I understand it, you accompanied President Tudjman to Siroki Brijeg on that day.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I accompanied President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Boban was present as well, I understand?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think from what I've seen, President Tudjman and not in this order but President Tudjman spoke, Mr. Boban spoke at some point, Mr. Susak spoke, and I think in addition, you spoke, yourself, that is speaking to the crowd that had assembled?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was customary for the president of the republic not to be followed by anyone, that he should be the last but I asked to be allowed to deliver a speech, and the speech I delivered was a pacifist one. I don't have its text but I tried to underscore that the war had to be brought to a stop, that that was in the interest of all and in particular, of course, of the Republic of Croatia because the entire south of Croatia had an interest in the end of the war, what with tourism and everything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I can assure you that we --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me just interject for a second. If we're going to use this document, a more fuller translation was provided by the Defence, I am told that at least in the very first page there is a section missing so I would refer, I would ask very kindly to use 1D02932, that was the Defence translation. I don't know whether Mr. Stringer is aware of that but it's the same document but it's a more fuller translation. That's only if he's going to go to the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well I am going to go to the document. What I have in my hand is a translation. Let me propose this, Mr. President, let's put them both together because I have something that's called a translation that was done by the CLSS, so I'm not sure what's meant by fuller and I don't have the document in front of me. Could I just --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I can put the very first page on it -- on the ELMO and we can all see that at least you had see that there is a paragraph that's missing completely. This is the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, let's do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We can look at also the original version, the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We've got actually a larger copy of the Croatian version that's been blown up for the witness in case he wants to read directly from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I can provide the part that is missing in the original version. I have no objection to the use of the document as long as it -- perhaps we can just refer the gentleman to the original document, that might save us sometime but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well he's got the original document. That's what I'm intending to do and maybe overnight we can put the two translations together and make sure that it's all there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's fine. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've been wanting to talk about unitary state and so this is where now I had intended to ask you some questions about that -- I'm referring Mr. Ambassador, I'm going to refer to a part of the speech in which President Tudjman says the following, in the beginning of the paragraph, it says, in his speech, President Tudjman also touched on. If you see those words in the original language, you'll see where I'm going. That's the paragraph. Then there is a quote attributed to President Tudjman. "In BiH, we have encountered a policy which has not been fully in accordance with Croatian interests. Part of the Muslim leadership believed that BiH could be developed as a unitary state in which they promised civil rights and civil freedoms but the Croatian people has enough experience with the entire former Yugoslavia in which the entire Croatian people was ostensibly promised such civil rights and freedoms which were used just as a screen for the oppression of the Croatian people." Then he continues, "Therefore, Croatia is interested in such a state set-up of Bosnia-Herzegovina if it is to survive in which the Croatian people in it are sovereign, that in areas in which it is a majority, there should be no other except Croatian rule." Then he goes on to talk about the Croats living here, that is in Siroki Brijeg, have the right to dual citizenship because you are an integral part of the Croatian people and because the existence of the Croatian state depends on your existence here." So it seems to me, Mr. Ambassador, that this passage sort of lays out very succinctly the differing policies, if you will. On the BH side, the policy is of a unitary state and on the Croatian side, the policy is of a state set-up in which Croatian people in Bosnia are sovereign and that where they are a majority, there is no other except Croatian rule. So my question to you is this: Isn't it true that President Tudjman was expressing the Croatian policy correctly on the 20th of May, 1993, when he said that in those places where Croatian people are the majority, they should have Croatian rule?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What would you like me to say to you? What do you want of me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your direct examination, you commented on various speeches and whether they were a reflection of the Croatian policy. So my question is whether this statement is also a reflection of the Croatian policy at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian state policy, and I reiterated that and described what it was on a couple of occasions, so the Croatian state policy vis-a-vis Bosnia-Herzegovina was in compliance with the constitution of the Republic of Croatia. The Croatian policy was based on friendship and mutual assistance between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croatian state policy provided support to the international community which was seeking federalisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Therefore, what you just mentioned that some Croats were in favour of the sort of unitary state, yes, there were such Croats, but those were the people in Sarajevo and elsewhere in Bosnia; however, the greatest majority was with the international community on this issue. I mentioned Ahtisaari, Vance-Owen Plan, Owen-Stoltenberg Plan, Cutileiro's plan, the contact group plan. All these plans favoured federalisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and this is mirrored in what President Tudjman said here. He didn't say anything different from what had already been laid down as permanent ground of the Croatian state policy towards Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So just so we're clear, then, the Croatian state policy was that for parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina in which Croats were the majority, there should be no other except Croatian rule. That was the official Croatian policy.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. And please allow me to say a few words about federations. There are various federations. There are the so-called symmetrical and asymmetrical federations. Yugoslavia was an asymmetrical federation in which there was only one who was in charge of everything. The same could have happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina. For that reason, the Croatian state policy was in favour of federation and it supported all the proposals in that direction. However, this federation was supposed to be a symmetrical one of the Swiss type. In other words, every constituent people would have equal rights. It shouldn't be a federation which one community would be dominating the rest. That would be an asymmetrical federation. President Tudjman was in favour of a symmetrical federation composed of three constituent peoples with equal rights within the federation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Within the Croatian or the Croat part of the federation then, it's the Croatian people and no other who would rule. That's the policy?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is completely untrue. You haven't grasped the gist of what I was saying. Speaking of federation, you always have minorities within such a structure and these minorities need to be protected. Therefore, there was never any mention of having something exclusively. Probably in areas where there were 90 per cent of Croats, they would probably have pretty complete rule but as the percentages in different municipalities varied, this implies that everyone had equal rights, Croats, Serbs and Bosniak Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I do apologise to my learned friend. Your Honour, of course it's a matter for my learned friend how he conducts cross-examination, but there has been an awful lot of testimony given by this witness as to the policy of the Croatian government. Now, if my learned friend states that the speech given on the 20th of May is inconsistent, well that should be put clearly and directly to the witness to comment on but otherwise, he has spent quite a considerable amount of time describing the policy; and I do suggest to my learned friend that if it's said that this statement, this speech of President Tudjman is inconsistent, that should be very squarely put to the witness to comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's our view, Mr. President, that the speech perfectly encapsulates Croatian policy in respect to the issues of sovereignty of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the exclusivity of Croatian rule in areas where Croats are a majority which is what's being said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's what I'm asking the witness to comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the difficulty of course is, and I won't waste too much time, but my learned friend is seeking to view a speech of two or three pages as a microcosm summary of the policy of the Republic of Croatia. Of course a number of transcripts and documents have been gone through which are before Your Honours and the witness has already stated very clearly describing all the sources why he states his opinion that the policy of his government is what was stated. If this says something that was different, I think it can be very easily dealt with rather than beating around the bush. That's my only comment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Perhaps one can soften the conflict a bit. President Tudjman is reported as having said here that the "Croatian parts should be under no other except Croatian rule." That means that the Croatian nationals in that area would form the government that put all this in question marks. It does not mean that there should be no rights for all non-Croats living in these provinces. So this is not tantamount to saying that it should be a dictatorial rule in complete neglect and denial of fundamental rights to those that would not be Croats in the Croat areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, can you answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Medjurgorje Agreement itself and what followed immediately thereafter which is the appointment of Mr. Prlic as the president of the government and the distribution in various cantons, the numbers of Croats and Muslims et cetera with regard to three provinces, the conclusion was made to distribute the presence of the Croats and the Muslims and the Serbs and if there were any other ethnic groups in towns, so I think that this is so transparent that what we have here is a proportional distribution of offices in various provinces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, we need to stop here because there is another hearing in this courtroom at quarter past 2.00 and I'm sitting on that particular trial as well. Tomorrow, you may proceed with that particular topic because you have some time left. I will ask the registrar to tell me exactly how much time you have left. Unless I'm mistaken, it's about an hour -- but let me give you the exact figure. You have used 3 hours and 6 minutes. You have 54 minutes left, give or take six minutes I had given you the time you had left when I said you had about an hour left. We'll reconvene tomorrow morning at 9.00.
